Our inspection kept us there until dark, when we left. On the way home my companion stopped briefly at the office of a daily newspaper.

I have mentioned my friend’s many peculiar whims, and that I indulged them—Je les ménageais, a phrase with no exact English equivalent. His present whim was to refuse any discussion of the murder until around noon the following day. Then, without warning, he asked whether I had noticed anything peculiar at the scene of the crime.

Something in the emphasis he gave the word “peculiar” made me shiver, though I could not have explained why.

“No, nothing peculiar,” I answered. “At least, nothing beyond what we both read in the newspaper.”

“The Gazette,” he said, “has failed, I fear, to convey the extraordinary horror of the affair. But set aside that paper’s empty opinions. It seems to me that people consider this mystery impossible to solve for the very reason they ought to find it easy: the outlandish nature of its details. The police are baffled by the apparent lack of a motive—not for the killing itself, but for its brutality. They also cannot reconcile the voices heard arguing with two other facts: that no one was found upstairs except the murdered Mademoiselle L’Espanaye, and that nobody could have escaped without being seen by the people coming up. The room’s extreme disorder, the body forced headfirst up the chimney, the dreadful mutilation of the old woman’s body—these things, together with those I have already mentioned and others I need not name, have completely defeated the authorities’ much-vaunted intelligence and left them unable to act. They have made the serious but common mistake of confusing the unusual with the difficult to understand. Yet it is precisely these departures from the ordinary that allow reason, if anything can, to find its way toward the truth. In an investigation like ours, the question should be less ‘What happened?’ than ‘What happened that has never happened before?’ Indeed, the ease with which I shall reach—or have reached—the solution to this mystery increases in direct proportion to how impossible the police think it is to solve.”

I looked at him in speechless amazement.

“At this moment,” he continued, glancing toward the door of our apartment, “I am expecting someone who, though perhaps not the person who committed these savage murders, must have been involved in their commission to some degree.”

Rising at an early hour, and once more managing to elude the watchfulness of my creditors, I hastened to the bookseller’s stall. There I spent the little cash I had on several volumes concerning Mechanics and Practical Astronomy. Once safely home with my purchases, I gave every unoccupied moment to reading them, and soon attained what I judged to be enough proficiency in these subjects to carry out my design. During the same period, I used every means to appease the three creditors who had so greatly troubled me. At last I succeeded, partly through the sale of sufficient household furniture to discharge half their demand, and partly through a pledge to pay the remainder when I completed a small undertaking I said I was planning, and in which I requested their assistance. By these devices, since they were ignorant fellows, I had little trouble in persuading them to serve my ends.

“With these arrangements settled, I managed, with my wife’s help and the utmost caution and secrecy, to sell my remaining property. I also borrowed a considerable sum in small amounts, on a variety of pretexts, with no regard whatever for how I might eventually repay it. Using the funds so obtained, I began purchasing, at intervals, lengths of exceedingly fine cambric muslin, each twelve yards long; twine; a supply of caoutchouc varnish; a large, deep wicker basket made to my order; and various other things required to construct and furnish a balloon of exceptional size. I instructed my wife to sew it together with all possible speed, and supplied every necessary detail of the method she was to follow. Meanwhile I fashioned the twine into netting of the proper dimensions, fitted it with a hoop and the requisite ropes, and purchased a quadrant, a compass, a telescope, an ordinary barometer altered in several important respects, and two less familiar astronomical instruments. Next, as opportunities offered, I carried by night to a secluded spot east of Rotterdam five iron-hooped casks, each capable of holding approximately fifty gallons, and another larger one; six suitably shaped tubes of tinned metal, three inches across and ten feet long; a supply of a certain metallic substance, or semi-metal, whose name I shall withhold; and twelve demijohns of a very common acid. The gas produced from these last materials has never been generated by anyone but myself—or, at any rate, never employed for a comparable purpose. I should have no objection to revealing the secret, except that it properly belongs to a resident of Nantz, in France, who disclosed it to me upon certain conditions.”

“If I may say so, Sir Walter,” said Mr. Shepherd one morning at Kellynch Hall, putting down the newspaper, “the timing is very much in our favor. Now that we have peace, all our rich naval officers will be coming ashore. They’ll all need homes. You couldn’t choose a better time to find tenants, Sir Walter—reliable tenants too. Many large fortunes were made during the war. If a wealthy admiral happened to approach us, Sir Walter—”

“He would be a very fortunate man, Shepherd,” Sir Walter replied. “That is all I can say. Kellynch Hall would certainly be a prize for him, the greatest prize of all, however many he has captured before. Wouldn’t it, Shepherd?”

Mr. Shepherd laughed at the joke, knowing that he must, and went on:

“I would point out, Sir Walter, that naval gentlemen are good people to do business with. I have some experience of their business dealings, and I must admit they are generous in their views and as likely to make good tenants as anyone you could find. So what I would suggest, Sir Walter, is this. Rumors of your plans may spread—we must consider that possibility, since we know how hard it is to keep one person’s affairs from the curiosity of others. Importance has its price. I, John Shepherd, could keep any family business private if I wished, because nobody would bother to watch me. But Sir Walter Elliot is observed by people whose attention may be very difficult to escape. Therefore I venture to say that, despite all our care, it would scarcely surprise me if some rumor of the truth got out. If that happens, as I was about to remark, offers will certainly follow. I should consider any proposal from a wealthy naval commander especially deserving of attention. And allow me to add that I can come here within two hours whenever you need me, to spare you the trouble of answering.”

Sir Walter merely nodded. Soon afterward, however, he stood and began walking about the room. He remarked sarcastically:

“I imagine very few naval gentlemen would expect to find themselves living in a house like this.”

“They would certainly look around and feel grateful for their luck,” said Mrs. Clay. She was there because her father had driven her over; nothing was supposed to benefit her health more than a drive to Kellynch. “But I agree entirely with my father that a sailor could make a very welcome tenant.”
